title: Thin margins need big sales
principle: A thin margin works only with high sales and low costs.

screens.text: Ravi keeps just ₹3 a cup at his chai stall and does well. His cousin keeps ₹3 a cup too, and is going broke.

screens.prompt: What is the big difference between the two stalls?
screens.why: Ravi sells 400 cups a day at the bus stand. His cousin sells 50 in a quiet lane.

screens.title: Thin margins
screens.text: A thin margin means you keep a little from each sale. It works only if you sell a lot and keep costs low.

screens.title: Ravi's day
screens.text: 400 cups × ₹3 = ₹1,200. Rent and his helper cost ₹600 a day. Ravi keeps ₹600 a day.

screens.prompt: His cousin sells 50 cups × ₹3 = ₹150 a day. His rent and helper also cost ₹600. What happens?
screens.why: ₹150 in margin, ₹600 in fixed costs. He is ₹450 short every day.

wrong.a: ₹150 is his margin. Rent and his helper still cost ₹600.
wrong.b: He needs 200 cups to break even. He sells 50.

screens.prompt: Rent and helper cost ₹600 a day. Each cup leaves ₹3. How many cups to break even?
screens.why: Fixed costs ÷ margin: ₹600 ÷ ₹3 = 200 cups a day.

wrong.b: 600 is the cost in rupees. Divide it by the ₹3 margin.
wrong.c: Divide the costs by the margin. Don't multiply.

screens.prompt: Does each thing help or hurt a stall that keeps ₹3 a cup?

items.text: A busy spot with many people
Buying milk in bulk for less
A second paid helper, with no extra sales
A quiet lane with few people
Serving fast, so the line keeps moving

screens.why: With ₹3 a cup, you need many buyers and low costs. Anything that adds cost or cuts buyers hurts.

screens.prompt: Milk gets dearer. Ravi now keeps ₹2 a cup, not ₹3. He still sells 400 cups. What is his daily profit now?
screens.why: 400 × ₹2 = ₹800, minus ₹600 of rent and helper = ₹200. Losing ₹1 a cup cut his profit by two thirds.

wrong.a: ₹600 was his profit at ₹3 a cup. Work it out at ₹2.
wrong.c: ₹800 is his margin. Take off the ₹600 of rent and helper.

screens.prompt: True or false: a thin margin is always bad.

options.label: False, it works with big sales and low costs
True, you should always keep a lot from each sale

screens.why: Ravi keeps ₹3 a cup and does well. It works because he sells 400 cups and keeps his costs low.

wrong.b: Ravi keeps only ₹3 a cup and still does well. What matters is how many he sells and what it costs him.

screens.setup: Ravi sells 400 cups a day and keeps ₹3 a cup. His rent and helper cost ₹600 a day. In a bigger shop with seats and a fan, rent and helper would cost ₹1,200 a day.
screens.question: Should Ravi move?

options.label: Yes. Seats and a fan will bring more people
options.outcome: Sales rise to 450 cups. After the higher costs, he keeps ₹150 a day, not ₹600.
options.why: 450 × ₹3 = ₹1,350. Take off ₹1,200 and only ₹150 is left.
options.better: Do the sum first. At ₹3 a cup, a big new cost needs many more cups.

options.label: Move, and raise chai to ₹12 a cup
options.outcome: Some buyers walk to the cheaper stall next door. His profit is now a guess.
options.why: A higher price might help, but he moved without doing the sum.
options.better: Work out first how many cups the new shop needs to pay for itself.

options.label: Do the sum first: how many cups pay ₹1,200?
options.outcome: He sees he would need 400 cups just to break even. He stays where he is.
options.why: ₹1,200 ÷ ₹3 = 400 cups. The higher costs would eat all of his ₹600 profit.

summary: A thin margin means you keep a little from each sale.
It works only with many sales and low costs.
With thin margins, small cost changes hit profit hard.

cards.front: You keep ₹2 a sale. Rent is ₹500 a day. How many sales a day just to pay rent?
Your margin is thin. A nicer shop doubles your rent. What do you check first?
options: How many more sales you need
cards.back: How many more sales you need. With a thin margin, every new cost needs many more sales.
